# Sigma-Algebra as Magma of Sets

## Definitions used

Let $X$ be a set, $\mathcal P(X)$ its power set.

**Magma of sets.** Let $I$ be an index set; for each $i\in I$ let $K_i$ be a set (the arity index set, possibly empty or infinite) and let $\odot_i:\mathcal P(X)^{K_i}\to\mathcal P(X)$ be a $K_i$-ary operation on $\mathcal P(X)$. A collection $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a *magma of sets for $(\odot_i)_{i\in I}$ on $X$* iff for every $i\in I$ and every family $(S_k)_{k\in K_i}$ with all $S_k\in\mathcal S$, we have $\odot_i\big((S_k)_{k\in K_i}\big)\in\mathcal S$. (For $K_i=\varnothing$, $\mathcal P(X)^{\varnothing}$ has exactly one element, the empty family, so $\odot_i$ is a constant $C_i\subseteq X$ and the condition says $C_i\in\mathcal S$.)

**$\sigma$-algebra.** $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ iff
- (SA1) $X\in\Sigma$;
- (SA2) $A\in\Sigma\implies X\setminus A\in\Sigma$;
- (SA3) for every countable family $(A_j)_{j\in J}$ ($J$ countable, i.e. finite or countably infinite) of elements of $\Sigma$, $\bigcup_{j\in J}A_j\in\Sigma$.

## Claim

Let $I=\{1,2,3\}$, $K_1=\varnothing$, $K_2=\{0\}$, $K_3=\mathbb N$, and define
- $\odot_1() = X$ (nullary),
- $\odot_2(A) = X\setminus A$ (unary),
- $\odot_3\big((A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\big)=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$ (countably-infinitary).

Each is a well-defined operation on $\mathcal P(X)$: $X\in\mathcal P(X)$, $X\setminus A\subseteq X$, and a union of subsets of $X$ is a subset of $X$.

Then for $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$: $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ iff $\Sigma$ is a magma of sets for $(\odot_1,\odot_2,\odot_3)$ on $X$. Hence the notion of $\sigma$-algebra is an instance of the notion of magma of sets.

## Proof

**($\Rightarrow$)** Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra.
- $i=1$: the only family is the empty one, and $\odot_1()=X\in\Sigma$ by (SA1).
- $i=2$: a family is a single $A\in\Sigma$; $\odot_2(A)=X\setminus A\in\Sigma$ by (SA2).
- $i=3$: a family is a sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$; $\mathbb N$ is countable, so $\bigcup_n A_n\in\Sigma$ by (SA3).

So $\Sigma$ is a magma of sets for these operations.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Let $\Sigma$ be a magma of sets for $(\odot_1,\odot_2,\odot_3)$.
- (SA1): closure under $\odot_1$ gives $X=\odot_1()\in\Sigma$.
- (SA2): for $A\in\Sigma$, closure under $\odot_2$ gives $X\setminus A\in\Sigma$.
- (SA3): let $(A_j)_{j\in J}$ be a family in $\Sigma$ with $J$ countable.
  - If $J=\varnothing$: $\bigcup_{j\in\varnothing}A_j=\varnothing=X\setminus X=\odot_2(X)\in\Sigma$, using $X\in\Sigma$ just shown.
  - If $J\neq\varnothing$: since $J$ is countable and nonempty there is a surjection $f:\mathbb N\to J$ (if $J$ is countably infinite take a bijection; if $J=\{j_0,\dots,j_{m-1}\}$ finite, set $f(n)=j_n$ for $n<m$ and $f(n)=j_0$ for $n\ge m$). Put $B_n=A_{f(n)}\in\Sigma$. Because $f$ is surjective, $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}B_n=\bigcup_{j\in J}A_j$ (every $B_n$ is some $A_j$, and every $A_j$ equals $B_n$ for some $n$ with $f(n)=j$). Closure under $\odot_3$ gives $\bigcup_{j\in J}A_j=\odot_3((B_n)_n)\in\Sigma$.

So $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra. $\blacksquare$

**Remark.** If one instead defines a $\sigma$-algebra with "$\Sigma\neq\varnothing$" in place of (SA1), the definitions agree: given $A\in\Sigma$, $X=A\cup(X\setminus A)$ is the union of the sequence $A, X\setminus A, X\setminus A,\dots$ of elements of $\Sigma$, so $X\in\Sigma$; conversely (SA1) gives $\Sigma\ne\varnothing$. Thus the characterization above holds for that definition too. Likewise, if (SA3) is stated only for sequences indexed by $\mathbb N$, closure under $\odot_3$ is literally that condition.
